speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thought it might be of some interest to hon. members to have a brief statement of our plans for the centennial year end program on parliament hill.
Members in all parts of the house have been very generous in their attendance at, support of and praise for centennial celebrations to date and I should like to thank them for all this. I hope there will be general agreement that we should close out the year on a high note-

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF CONCLUDING EVENTS ON PARLIAMENT HILL
speechtext:
As I say, I hope there will be general agreement that we should close out
the year on a high note, pointing clearly toward the promise of the second century which lies ahead of us.
To that end the centennial commission has arranged for two major ceremonies to be held this month on parliament hill. The first of these will take place this Friday, December 8, beginning at 3.30 p.m. Its prime purpose will be to launch a national "help a child" program to encourage young Canadians through their schools to make a special contribution to assistance programs for children in less fortunate parts of the world. I should hope the house would agree with me that it is appropriate, especially at this time of year, that we turn the accent of our centennial celebrations, which have been mainly introspective to date, to the broader world horizon and to recognition of the fortunate place we as Canadians have in that horizon.
While the ceremony on Friday will include particular reference to the "help a child" program for the national capital area, this is, I should stress, a national program, and centennial commission officials already are co-operating with the provinces in encouraging participation by schools and school children from one end of the country to the other.
While in a sense, Mr. Speaker, this is a very solemn undertaking, we have planned Friday's ceremony to take into account as well the festive season which is upon us. It will be centred about the lighting of the monster Christmas trees on parliament's lawns and will include a fireworks display, appearances by several National Hockey League stars and entertainers, and carol singing; as well, I understand, as a special visit from that elderly gentleman known as St. Nicholas.
The second ceremony, as might be expected, will be to formally close out the year on the evening of December 31. This occasion will feature an address to the nation via television by His Excellency the Governor General, as well as a religious ceremony, choral singing and a fireworks display. It also will provide a final focus on the centennial flame, which has shone so brightly as a beacon of our celebrations throughout the year.

December 4, 1967
Questions
As a final note I might add that during the period between December 15 and 30 the commission also has arranged for regular performances such as were held on the hill during the summer months, to be staged by major bands and choirs from the national capital area.
Mr. Speaker, while both the major ceremonies will be televised by the C.B.C., it certainly is our hope and desire that as many Canadians as possible will come to parliament hill to share directly in these events with us. I would then like to issue a very special invitation to all members of this chamber and the other place, all of whom will be receiving written invitations to both events, to help us celebrate the close of this most eventful year.

subtopic: OT-4 ENGINE DEVELOPMENT PROGRAM
OT-4 ENGINE DEVELOPMENT PROGRAM
speechtext:
1.	How much money has the Canadian government provided for the OT-4 development program conducted by Orenda Limited of Malton, Ontario?
2.	How much money has the United States government provided for the OT-4 development program conducted by Orenda Limited of Malton, Ontario?
3.	Have any of the OT-4 engines been completed and put into use and, if so (a) how many have been completed and what use is being made of them (b) what is the record of performance of these engines in comparison with other engines of similar horsepower?
4.	Why did the Canadian government decide to discontinue financial assistance to the OT-4 program?
5.	What were the "other developments" referred to in the answers given by the Minister of Industry to questions asked in the house on October 17, 1967, as recorded on page 3167 of Hansard for that date?
6.	What specific steps are being taken to ensure that the engineering design team at Orenda Limited remain in Canada?
December 4, 1967

speakeroldname: Hon. C. M. Drury (Minister of Industry):
speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
subtopic: OT-4 ENGINE DEVELOPMENT PROGRAM
speechtext:
1.	At the time Canadian government financial support was withdrawn, i.e., 30 September, 1967, the Canadian government had expended $10,090,000.
2.	As of 30 September, 1967, the United States had expended $5,593,000.
3.	(a) As of 30 September, 1967, 14 engines had been built and two others were in assembly stage. Of the 14 engines built, seven have been used for test-bed development at Orenda, and seven for trial installations. The seven installations are: two in United States navy minesweepers; three in United States army tracked vehicles and one, plus one spare replacement, in a commercial truck, (b) Not being a production engine it is difficult to compare OT-4 performance with other types of engines of similar horsepower. In terms of its performance objectives, however, the OT-4 had not achieved its design power output and fell short of its target on specific fuel consumption but its reliability was about normal for its development status. It was not expected, however, as a production engine, to be sufficiently competitive with the current diesel engines of comparable power in respect to specific fuel consumption and selling price per horsepower.
4.	Following appraisal of a comprehensive market study undertaken by an independent consulting organization of Orenda marketing plans, of United States military engine requirements, and of the status of the OT-4 development program, the Department of Industry concluded that: (a) The OT-4 was not expected, by 1975, to be fully competitive with diesel and other engines in terms of cost and performance; (b) While there might be, in time, an adequate overall market potential for industrial gas turbines in the OT-4 power range, the volume achievable by the OT-4 would not, in the opinion of the department, be commensurate with the development and preproduction investment involved; (c) A partnership arrangement between Orenda and a company having the necessary skills in volume production, international marketing and after sales service was considered by both Orenda and the Department of Industry to be necessary. No such arrangement appeared to be within reach; (d) An adequate industrial return to the Canadian economy on the proposed continuing Canadian government investment in the program did not appear to be achievable.
This decision of the Canadian government to discontinue financial assistance was taken
Questions
in the light of the fact that neither the United States government nor Orenda were prepared to put additional funds in the program.
5.	The OT-4 design was conceived in the early 1960's and during its development cycle many product and performance improvements were incorporated. In recent years, however, the age of the design concept placed constraints on the developer to incorporate advanced componentry and materials without major redesign. It is considered that, by 1975, the earliest time by which the OT-4 would be available in quantity for the industrial turbine commercial market, simpler and less expensive engines of comparable performance will be available based on more advanced components and materials.
6.	Efforts by my department and industry aimed at retaining the OT-4 engineering design team in Canada are continuing. To date, approximately 25 per cent of the OT-4 professional engineering personnel have been offered alternate positions within the Orenda organization and another 45-55 per cent have been or will be offered positions with a number of other Canadian companies.

Ocean, coastal and inshore minesweepers and minehunting ships are used in mine countermeasures. subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY BOARD POWERS, PROVIDE FOR APPEAL DIVISION, ETC.
speechtext:
that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act to clarify certain powers of the board; to provide for the appointment of two vicechairmen in lieu of one; to provide for an appeal division of the board; and to provide further for certain changes in connection with the administration of the act.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Batten in the chair.

maintopic: INDUSTRIAL RELATIONS AND DISPUTES INVESTIGATION ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY BOARD POWERS, PROVIDE FOR APPEAL DIVISION, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the amendments proposed in the resolution take cognizance of the reality and of the force of very important changes that are current in the Canadian industrial relations environment. The purpose of the amendments is to clarify the powers and to facilitate the work of the Canada Labour Relations Board in the light of these significant changes to which I have referred.
Most hon. members will recall that the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act, commonly known as the I.R.D.I. act, came into force on September 1, 1948. It is now in its twentieth year without amendment of any kind. The Canada Labour Relations Board was established on the effective date of the legislation, September 1, 1948. I might say it was established as the successor organization to the Wartime Labour Relations Board which did such a good job for Canada during the war and the important post-war years.
This board administers the provisions of the act concerning the certification of bargaining units and, because this work takes a fair amount of time, I mention also the revocation of certifications and the review of earlier decisions. It also deals with the writing of provisions for incorporation into collective agreements that fix a procedure for the final settlement of disputes concerning the meaning or violation of such agreements. It also
Industrial Relations Act deals with the investigation of complaints referred to it by the Minister of Labour that one party or another has failed to bargain collectively in good faith.
The board consists of a chairman, one vice chairman and eight members, four of whom represent the employees and the other four represent the employers. The present chairman has had a board background of experience in this field. He has served as deputy minister of labour and as vice chairman of the Canada Labour Relations Board before taking over its chairmanship in 1964. The vice chairman of the board is a senior civil servant. He is the deputy director of investigation and research in the Department of the Registrar General. The vice-chairman does not participate in the work of the board if the chairman is available. He acts as the presiding officer only in the absence of the chairman.
The history of this board is rather interesting. During the war years there were four labour groups of appreciable size in this country, the old Trades and Labour Congress, the Canadian Congress of Labour, the railway unions, and what were called the Canadian Catholic unions in the province of Quebec. There were Teamsters and other organized groups, but the four that I have mentioned were the four major groups of organized labour in this country.
When the Canada Labour Relations Board started to function in September, 1948, representation on it was substantially the same as on the Wartime Labour Relations Board. There was one representative of the Canadian Trades and Labour Congress, one of the railway unions, one of the Canadian Congress of Labour, and one of the Canadian and Catholic unions. When the Canadian Labour Congress, the C.L.C., came into being it provided the unions affiliated with it with three representatives, whereas the Canadian and Catholic unions, now the C.N.T.U., continued to have only one representative.
During the 20-year period that it has been functioning the board has done yeoman service for the people of Canada. It might be said that the philosophy of the board has been the administration of the provisions of the act and the determination of each particular case on its merits. During these 20 years the growth of collective bargaining has greatly increased the work of the board. I shall give some figures to illustrate this. During the period prior to 1966 the average number of applications dealt with by the board per annum, in round figures, was

December 4, 1967
Industrial Relations Act about 100. In the last two years applications have averaged in excess of 140 per annum, an increase of roughly 40 or 45 per cent. In addition, and this is something I stress, rivalries among labour unions have placed increased pressures on the board.
The amendments covered by this resolution are designed to assist the board to deal with these new developments. I think I should state at this stage that no change in the representative character of the board is proposed, such as the three representatives from the C.L.C. and its affiliates and one representative from the C.N.T.U. If the resolution and the bill based thereon are accepted, the board will continue to represent equally the interests of employers and employees.
The amendments, however, do propose some new elements. First, they are designed to clarify the provisions in the act relating to the appropriateness of bargaining units. They also deal with the character of unions involved in applications for certification or designation.
It is also proposed that there be two vicechairmen of the board as against one under the present act, and that the board be empowered to sit in panels. With the increase in work to which I have referred, the desirability of having the board sit in panels, as do so many of our courts, has become self-evident. It is that such a practical board, representing the people with whom the board's work is concerned, should be given the widest possible discretion to discover, on the basis of its practical experience, the best modus vivendi and modus operandi in the labour relations field, and the best way in which to do the work which will encourage peace and minimize the possibility of labour unrest.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this resolution is obviously the result of pressure put on the government by the labour unions which complain that they are badly treated or misunderstood by the Canada Labour Relations Board.
For example, the C.N.T.U. has complained many times about the Canada Labour Relations Board, and today the government is presenting the following resolution, and I quote:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act to clarify certain powers of the board; to provide for the appointment of two vice-chairmen in lieu of one; to provide for an appeal division of the board; and to provide further for certain changes in connection with the administration of the act.
The hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis), who just resumed his seat, said that this resolution may have been introduced to please a given group or trade union. He was probably referring to the C.N.T.U. which had difficulties with the C.B.C. on a few occasions, but he did not want or he avoided to mention the C.N.T.U.
A moment ago, he expressed his lack of confidence in the introduction of a bill to improve labour and industrial relations, to clarify certain powers of the board, to provide for the appointment of two vice chairmen in lieu of one, and also to provide further for certain changes in connection with the administration of the act.
Mr. Chairman, we find it difficult now to discuss this proposed measure which will be introduced, since it is not the bill itself that has been put before us but the resolution preceding the introduction of the bill in the house. Therefore, even if it is possible to guess at some of the provisions of the bill which will follow the resolution, we must wait until the bill is introduced in parliament to discuss them.
The hon. member for York South says that this bill should put a stop to the increasing number of strikes in Canada, but we are now witnessing rather difficult industrial relations, labour-management relations in England. In fact, there have been strikes in the nationalized railways as well as in other nationalized or public industries. There again, the theory of socialism, of the labour state was applied, and that does not seem to have settled many things. To have, in Canada, an organization, an industrial relations board or an employer-employee relations board that would act
Industrial Relations Act efficiently, study both sides of the question, consider objectively the existing problems or those that might crop up, I believe it would be a good omen.
I also think the minister is right in proposing his resolution and seeking authority to introduce a bill which we may discuss with all the necessary leeway and move amendments if we are not satisfied with its contents.
I believe we should support the immediate adoption of this proposed resolution.
Mr. Chairman, I shall await the bill which the Minister of Labour (Mr. Nicholson) intends to introduce before making further comments.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this afternoon the Minister of Labour introduced a resolution to amend the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act and gave specific details of the content of the bill and the purpose of the resolution. He pointed out that this act has not been amended since 1948. He also pointed out that the realities of the economy and of the labour market in Canada have changed considerably in these 20 years. He stated that the main purpose of the resolution and the bill to follow was to meet two problems, the increasing rivalry between trade unions, and the increasing work load of the board.
I was somewhat surprised to hear the hon. member for Ontario, a former minister of labour and chief critic of the Conservative party on labour matters, ask who wants amendments. He stated he did not know anybody who wanted the act amended and he questioned the resolution and the proposed changes. It seems to me the hon. member for Ontario must restrict his reading to English newspapers in Ontario. As one who would be a natural choice for minister of labour if he were re-elected to office, which is doubtful, he should be aware of the widespread criticism of the present composition of the board and the resultant injustice to French Canada in the set-up of the board.
While his leader was in French Canada over the week end preaching that we must give consideration to the two founding language groups in Canada, the hon. gentleman is telling us here that there is no criticism of this act in Canada. I should like to read a brief extract from the memorandum submitted to the government by the Confederation

December 4, 1967
Industrial Relations Act of National Trade Unions in which it is stated:
The act must be amended in such a way that when the two organizations-
The C.N.T.U. and the C.L.C.
-are in conflict over a question on which the board must make a decision, the two unions be represented equally.
This means in practice, Mr. Chairman, that there must be more representatives from the C.N.T.U. and less from the C.L.C. The minister has stated that there will be no change in representation on the labour relations board but that new methods would be devised to deal with this problem.
I think we must do something to correct the great feeling of injustice on the part of many trade unionists in the province of Quebec in relation to the board. One long-standing principle of British justice is that justice must not only be done but that it must be seen to be done. According to a great number of people in the trade union movement in Quebec, justice is definitely not seen to be done as far as the Canadian Labour Relations Board is concerned, especially in the matter of jurisdictional disputes.
As we all know, there are four representatives from labour and four representatives from the employers on the board. Of the four labour representatives, two are from the Canadian Labour Congress, one is from the railway unions and the fourth is from the C.N.T.U. In some of the decisions about which the C.S.N. has complained, three of the representatives-the two C.L.C. representatives plus the representative of the railways -have voted against the position taken by the C.N.T.U.
There is also another reason that the number of chairmen should be increased. At the moment, of the nine members of the Canada Labour Relations Board only three are French speaking. If there is going to be equal justice in this country for those who are French speaking as well as for those who are English speaking, then there must be a greater degree of bilingualism among the members of the Canada Labour Relations Board. So far there has not been this degree of bilingualism, the type of bilingualism that the leader of the official opposition has been preaching about since his election but which his chief labour critic does not seem to favour too much. At the present moment, Mr. Chairman, if a union which basically is comprised of French speaking members appears before the Canada Labour Relations Board it must

engage a lawyer to represent it who speaks good English. It must make sure that all its representations to the board are understood by the board.
With regard to the method of appointment to the board, it seems to me that while persons from English speaking Canada can be appointed to the board without the necessity of their knowing French, a French speaking member must know English before he can be appointed. Is this the type of justice we are trying to promote when we speak, as the Conservatives do, about respect for the two founding language groups in Canada?
No, Mr. Chairman, there is dissatisfaction with the present setup of the Canada Labour Relations Board. It is not simply that we must make amendments to satisfy one group; we must also be sure we have fair play and that we have justice, especially in the matter of jurisdictional disputes, from the Canada Labour Relations Board.
The Canadian Labour Congress dealt with this question in their last brief to the government of Canada. On page 28 this statement appears:
We wish to reiterate the position taken by us before the cabinet committee that we do not propose to accede to any change in the composition of the board which would reduce the number of congress nominees and add to that of the confederation. We say this secure in the knowledge that we are indisputably the major trade union centre not only in Canada as a whole but in the province of Quebec as well. The congress alone has members in every part of Canada. We do not propose to subordinate ourselves to a minor organization merely to satisfy the aspirations of its leaders.
As far as I can see, Mr. Chairman, legislation of this nature is not meant to satisfy the aspirations of a minority but to bring about greater fair play and justice. It also seems to me that the Canadian Labour Congress, which is the major labour group in Canada, should not condone the principle of the majority dictating to the minority. There should be justice for minority groups in Canada and recognition of their point of view by boards set up by the federal government.
I should like to quote some of the points made by the C.S.N. in an addendum to their brief to the federal government last year. They say:
We have frequently had considerable difficulty before the C.L.R.B. A federal body must accept the realities that exist in the country. If this is not done, and if the employees concerned by this matter do not obtain justice, the C.N.T.U. will seriously question its participation in the federal organizations, in the future-
December 4, 1967

A federal body like the C.L.R.B. cannot directly or indirectly be made the tool to shackle a free union for the benefit of an American union that is unacceptable to its members.
The latter point has reference to a situation where a large number of French speaking employees of the C.B.C. in Quebec rejected the previous union which was dominated by U.S. interests.
I suggest that there is much room for improvement in our labour relations law. The government has appointed the Woods commission to bring forward far reaching changes in the law, but in the meanwhile there are other changes that can be made to effect greater justice and fair play to other groups in Canada, whether they be from Quebec or from outside Quebec.
The minister must be commended for bringing forward this measure. I know that all members of trade unions, whether they belong to C.L.C. affiliated unions or to C.N.T.U. affiliated unions, will appreciate a greater flexibility in questions involving jurisdictional disputes, panels and appeals, thus ensuring a more complete hearing and greater justice than is the case at the moment. This will do much to unify and consolidate the labour movement in Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to answer immediately the point made by the hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace who has just resumed his seat. I doubt that anybody in this chamber would object in the slightest to any change which might be necessary in order to give fair representation on this board to French speaking members. If that were the purpose of the bill to be introduced by this resolution and if it were clearly set out in that form, I doubt that any member of this house would have any objection to raise.
But it is not necessary to change the legislation in order to achieve the admirable objective stated by the hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace. There is no need whatever to bring in legislation for that purpose. The government already has the necessary authority to do what is described. There is nothing in the act to prevent it. But if this were the purpose of the bill, why does the minister not tell us? He mentioned no such thing.
The answer is, of course, that the bill does not do what the hon. member has suggested. It does not provide for any additional French speaking members. Indeed, it provides for nothing which relates to the observations
Industrial Relations Act made by the hon. member who has just resumed his place. I can only suggest that this is another red herring introduced to prevent our looking very closely at the legislation.
I wish to deal with just one aspect of the resolution and that is the proposal to set up an appeal division. I cannot imagine anything more damaging to sensible decisions in connection with labour legislation than the setting up of an appeal division, a hierarchy of appeals within one single board, especially when this board is dealing with a relatively narrow subject matter. I myself had a good deal of experience a number of years ago with the first labour relations court ever set up in Canada, the Ontario labour relations court which was brought into existence in 1943. I appeared as counsel for a number of the parties before that court. The court did its best. On a number of occasions it rendered decisions favourable to labour, decisions which were regarded as fair.
My point is this. Representatives of both labour and management were agreed that the proceedings of the court were utterly unsuitable for dealing with labour relations matters, and the court was abolished within a short time. What were the reasons for doing so? They have already been indicated by my hon. friend from York South. They are that it is absolutely essential when dealing with labour relations to establish a tribunal which can act quickly and can act on practical grounds, not on the basis of legalistic considerations.
What is the purpose of the legislation now proposed? It is to provide a board which can promote the process of collective bargaining and lead to industrial peace. The main function of this board is to determine who shall represent the workers. If there is to be a hierarchy of appeal procedures set up within this board and if, as is possible, the position is made still more complex by further appeals to the legal courts of the land, we may easily reach a situation which has already been reached in the United States where after a union has applied for certification legal proceedings can drag on for four years, by the end of which time it is possible that the organization concerned no longer exists or the parties have long settled their differences without benefit of the procedures of the law. It is totally wrong to introduce here arguments which are appropriate to the constitution of courts. We are not constituting a court in this instance. Yet we create, in

December 4, 1967
Industrial Relations Act effect, a court if we induce public spirited people from outside to hear appeals from decisions of the Canadian Labour Relations Board or any division of it.
The minister showed his tendency to think in lawyer-like terms when he referred to the Supreme Court of Canada and suggested that the Canadian Labour Relations Board needed additional panels because they are needed in the Supreme Court of Canada. But the Supreme Court of Canada has to hear appeals in connection with totally different systems of law and it is obviously appropriate in this instance that the court, or the majority of the court, should be trained in whichever legal system they are administering. But here we are dealing with industries which are by definition national industries of national scope. It would be an extraordinary thing were two different groups dealing with the same code, the same system, to apply it in different ways in different parts of the country.
Above all, the proposal to introduce a hierarchy of appeals represents the introduction into the field of labour relations of a concept which has no place there. It could only lead to delay, confusion, frustration and jealousy; it could only make the whole operation fail to do its job in promoting peaceful labour conditions.
When I see such poor reasons advanced in favour of this resolution as those which have been given us so far, I am bound to repeat the question asked by my hon. friend from York South: What are the indirect purposes behind the introduction of this resolution? I do not think we have been given any frank statement. The hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace suggested a grievance on the part of the province of Quebec. If the purpose of the resolution is to remedy this grievance, let us hear from the minister and consider whether there is a better way of doing it than by messing up legislation which has worked reasonably well in the past. We are all interested in the terms of the bill itself but I express a great deal of reserve about this legislation, relieved only by the undertaking that the subject matter will be referred to a committee of the house where it can be fully examined before second reading.

Mr. Chairman, I did not intend to take part in the discussion at this stage. I thought we would have the opportunity of speaking on second reading. If this bill is referred to a committee, I hope it will

be after the house had had the opportunity to decide on the principle of the bill. However, as we do not seem to be quite decided yet, I should like to make a few remarks.
It was mentioned, that the field of labour relations is very specialized. It has brought about the establishment of special courts, either for certification or for conciliation. Surely, as was mentioned, the problems involved are not only legal problems, but first of all economic and social problems of a very special character which ordinary courts are not prepared to consider objectively.
In discussing such a bill, however, one can be sentimental or even angelic Mr. Chairman but I think that, at the present time, it is not the government that is evading the issue but those very people who would have this house believe that arbitration boards, labour relations boards are not what they are, that is to say, organizations representing interest groups. And that is not hypocrisy; that is just the way it is.
It happens, for instance, that labour representatives on conciliation boards, if my information is good, never signed a minority report favourable to the employer, and I have no recollection of having seen a representative of the employer signing a minority report favourable to the workers. Even if they are very objective, that never happened.
I have never seen, in the Canada Labour Relations Board, members of the Canadian Labour Congress voting against one of their unions concerned, when it was in conflict with another union. It happened that the members of the Canadian Labour Congress divided when they had to deal with two requests coming from their own central committee, but never in the case of one request only coming from a union under the congress. Evidently, it is entirely coincidental.
There is, of course, that objectivity the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis) mentioned. However, his objectivity is only in his head because in practice-and apart from that-the act did not want those people to be objective in the sense that is expected of a judge in a regular court. In fact, there was so little desire for them to be objective that the board was set up on a parity basis: four representatives of the employers on one side and four representatives of the workers on the other. Why was that? If those people are objective, why are they chosen thus on a parity basis in each group? Because it is a well known fact-and the hon. member for York South knows it as well as I do-that
December 4, 1967

those people represent various interests. It does not mean that they are dishonest, but they are there to represent the interests of their central committee and their affiliated groups and when they do that, they comply with the spirit of the act.
Why say in this house that we are trying to destroy the present objective character of the Canada Labour Relations Board?

speechtext: Because it is the truth.

maintopic: INDUSTRIAL RELATIONS AND DISPUTES INVESTIGATION ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY BOARD POWERS, PROVIDE FOR APPEAL DIVISION, ETC.
speechtext:
It is not true. We want simply to make sure that some present-day wrongs cannot be committed by the board whose members represent interested parties, which is quite normal.
Moreover, I think, personally, that such a representative character of labour relations boards should be maintained, for this is a tried and true formula in the labour relations field. However to say that we would destroy the objective character of the board, just because we want, in some cases, to balance out the board in order to prevent any wrongdoing, is just too much. This argument would hold, perhaps, for someone who has never seen a labour relations board in operation, but I disagree, being quite aware that the people who represented my local within the Canada Labour Relations Board spoke for my local, just like others spoke for the F.Q.W. and employers' representatives spoke for management. In my estimation, there has never been any question of some other form of objectivity in the act.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, to talk about a subterfuge, is really to go a little far. In fact, when a labour union, which is not represented on the board or has a minority representation, comes before this body and sees its case lost from the beginning or cannot obtain justice, because of the interplay of interests and the natural tendencies and concepts of the representatives, I think that any impartial and fair person should be ready to reconsider the structure of this board-bearing in mind the cases I have referred to-in order that all the Canadian citizens, all the organizations-not only a few, but all-may be assured of a fair treatment by the Canada Labour Relations Board.

Mr. Chairman, I am not speaking only of the unions affiliated to the C.N.T.U. but of all those which, by accident or in conformity with the constitution of the board, are not represented on this board, because-and our friends in the New Demo-
Industrial Relations Act cratic party surely know this as well as I-there are various interests in the labour field. There are the interests of the unions and those of the employers. Because of the differences which exist between the labour unions in Canada, there are presently many cases where the employers, and not the union representatives, decide what union will be recognized. As soon as the union group is divided, the balance of power rests with the management. Is that normal? Is that what we want? Is that the power we want the management to have? The right to make the decisions for their employees, for their union? The opposite is true in other sectors of the economy, Mr. Chairman.
Without mentioning any name, I know that when an employer enjoys a normal and friendly relationship with a labour organization, it is customary for that employer, within the Canadian Labour Relations Board, if that organization has some interests to promote, to support-unless there are policy objections-the union applying for certification, because it is, of course, indirectly in its interest. It is normal. We wanted it that way, so let's not bring up questions of objectivity.
Why, Mr. Chairman, are ministers asked to divest themselves of private interests, of directorships in companies? Is it because the House of Commons does not trust the objectivity of the present ministers or those who might be appointed eventually? It is not for that reason, but because if they had private interests, their objectivity would be in danger.
That does not mean that the members of the board are dishonest people; let no one put in our mouth things we have never said. Personally, I think that the members of the board are honest people, whether they belong to the Canadian Labour Congress or they are appointed by employers. I think that most of them-all those I know, anyway-are people upon whom I would rely in any case, except in cases where they have private interests. It is normal then for the legislator to balance the representation within the board so that the interests at stake are not sacrified to the process of law. That is all we want to do; we are seeking to preserve the principle of representation of the parties concerned within that board. However, it is impossible to have them all represented on the C.L.R.B.
[DOT] (5:00 p.m.)
There is, at present, the main labour organization, the Canadian Labour Congress. On the other hand, there is the C.N.T.U. which has only one representative. There are

December 4, 1967
Industrial Relations Act also other unions, which may be bona fide unions or still to be established, and which are not represented on the C.L.R.B. Does this mean that because they are not represented on the C.L.R.B. they will not have the same privileges as the unions affiliated to the C.L.C.? Does this mean that some citizens, some free organizations in Canada will not be treated like the others? Does the house want to treat various groups differently? I do not think so.
I know full well that certain groups were defeated before the Canada Labour Relations Board strictly bcause they did not have representatives to fight for their interests. It is obvious. Everyone knows it. Look around and see how the world of labour insists that it must be represented everywhere. Is it because labour fears a lack of objectivity on the part of those who are appointed by the government? No. It is because they have interests, points of view and is just what those boards need.
Mr. Chairman, the purpose of this resolution is precisely to see to it that the structure of the board will ensure fairness, not just accidentally, but because it is made up of good men; indeed, its structure should at least ensure balance in every case, especially in cases of conflict.
Now, Mr. Chairman, it has been mentioned

It is in the resolution before us, Mr. Chairman-excuse me if I remained standing-where it is mentioned that an appeal division of the board will be provided. For the benefit of the hon. member for York South, this changes the structure, as a matter of fact, it is a new structure. That is why I say that we have tried to create a structure that would really guarantee impartiality.
As far as I am concerned, Mr. Chairman, I am sure of one thing, and it is that a body, like the Canada Labour Relations Board, or any other body set up to render justice in Canada, must provide guarantees of impartiality, and this board, just like any government department, must not belong to any

particular organization. Nobody has the right to monopolize the labour relations boards or any other organization dealing with labour relations. Unfortunately at the present time, it is too often the case. This is the condition which we wanted to correct.
There has been some reference earlier to the splitting of competing unions and to the fostering of division in labour ranks.
Mr. Chairman, I feel that the arguments of upholders of labour unions are very weak when they depend on the law to bring Canadian unions together. I question very much their judgment and their wisdom. The labour movement itself can unify not only its structure but also its bargaining units. When the labour movement must rely on legislation to achieve such unity, I find it extremely weak and disappointing, because under this resolution and later, under the bill, nothing will prevent the unity of the labour movement from trying to have bargaining units of the size they choose.
On the other hand, efforts are made to maintain privileges and particularly to cover the voices of some who are being heard and who, on occasion, are being flattered for other purposes. But when a practical problem arises, it does not work any more, it is good only for statements of principles.
When the special status and the two nations theory or the awareness of various environments in Canada are involved, it always goes well in principle, but as soon as an attempt is made to alter legislation so as to eliminate excessive privileges, to correct abuses, then the question of objectivity and the traditions in the labour world are invoked.
To my mind, Mr. Chairman, the greatest tradition in the labour world is to seek justice not only for such and such a labour organization but for all labour organizations and for all workers.

speechtext:
I still think it would have been better had the ministers compared notes before they spoke rather than attempt to rationalize their speeches afterward. The main purpose of the speech of the Minister of Labour seemed to be to indicate that there were administrative difficulties and a backlog of work and certain other problems to be solved. The Minister of Manpower and Immigration came clean and told us that in his view the general purpose of the legislation is to alter the balance of labour representation so far as the Canada Labour Relations Board is concerned.
The main thing that is wrong with this legislation is that it has been drawn in a dishonest fashion. I say to the Minister of Manpower and Immigration that he is trying to have it both ways. Either the appeal provision and the panels that the Minister of Labour proposes to set up do what the Minister of Manpower and Immigration wants, namely, redress the imbalance, in which case the Minister of Labour is misleading us, or they do not, in which case the Minister of Manpower and Immigration is misleading those who wish this to be done.
I suggest that the proposal by the Minister of Labour that this matter not proceed to second reading but rather be referred to the committee on labour and employment is a good one. I believe in that case we could persuade the government that the bill ought to be torn up and drawn over again. If the purpose of the bill is what the Minister of Manpower and Immigration says it is, then
Industrial Relations Act let it be drawn in that way. If there is a backlog which cannot be taken care of by extra days of sittings in the month or if there is a need to get other people on the board to represent other groups, then let them increase the size of the board. The more we look at the proposal and the more the minister tries to justify it the more this legislation appears to be one of these attempts to do indirectly what the government is not prepared to do directly. There is another point I should like to make when we are discussing the amendments of the Minister of Labour. We want to complain bitterly and strenuously about the things the Minister of Labour is not bringing forward. May I remind him that four years ago this very month, in November, 1963, his predecessor, the then minister of labour and present Minister of National Health and Welfare, assured us that at the earliest possible moment the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act would be brought before parliament for amendment with respect to matters that needed amending.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
May I remind the minister also that two years ago this month, in November, 1965, the Freedman commission published its report in which there was spelled out a whole new concept of the rights of workers with respect to their jobs. I need not go into the details of the Freedman commission report. In the main, while admitting that management had certain rights, it stated that when it came to technological changes the least that should be done is to make them negotiable with the workers. The right of the workers to their jobs was spelled out very clearly in the

December 4, 1967
Industrial Relations Act Freedman report. We tried to get something done about that report when we had other legislation before us but we were put off and told that this was something which was related to the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act and could come in the future. Here we are, two years since the Freedman report and four years since the Minister of National Health and Welfare in his former portfolio assured us that this act would be amended, and we now have before us only the unnecessary proposals mentioned today.
In the meantime the urgency of these other problems has grown. Only a few days ago my colleague, the hon. member for Winnipeg North, asked a question about what was happening to a skilled group of employees, namely the railway telegraphers in the city of Winnipeg and other places who are being laid off because of technological changes. The purport of my colleague's question was, will the government in the near future be bringing forward legislation to implement the recommendations of the Freedman commission? This question was asked on November 27 and is recorded in Hansard on page 4716. The minister replied:
Mr. Speaker, no legislation is contemplated for introduction at this session to implement any such recommendations.
We have heard questions today about layoffs by the Canadian Pacific Railway to take place between Christmas and New Year's. Also alluded to today by the leader of this group was the question of whether the timing of these lay-offs between Christmas and New Year's will affect the right of these men to pay for Christmas day, Boxing day and New Year's day. This brings up the whole question of the difficulties the Department of Labour has had in administering the Canada Labour (Standards) Code, particularly with regard to both general and annual holidays.
The minister may say that this is another piece of legislation and not the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act. Let me remind him that not only do some of us think that these various pieces of legislation are related, but when the Canada Labour (Safety) Code was passed by this parliament last session it contained section 30 which gave the commission that is revising the statutes of Canada the power to put into one statute of Canada the Canada Labour (Standards) Code, the Canada Labour (Safety) Code, the Female Employees Equal Pay Act, the Canada Fair Employment Practices Act

and the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act. In other words, by bringing that section before us the minister himself admitted that these various pieces of legislation are integrally related.
It is in respect of some of these other pieces of legislation that we are having difficulty in interpreting the Canada Labour (Standards) Code and in getting the government to move on the Canada Labour (Safety) Code. Something desperately needs to be done about these matters. We get nothing out of the minister about these other problems, yet he comes along today with this piece of legislation that is totally unnecessary.
May I take a moment or two longer to emphasize the seriousness of the problem created by technological change and what it means to some employees. I mentioned the small group of railroad telegraphers who have been told by the C.N.R. that their positions will be eliminated. The employees concerned feel that this is in violation of a clause of their contract and that they should be protected against this kind of thing by labour legislation. I also think they should be protected. In the meantime all the company says to these employees, who at the moment are skilled persons with average earnings of $3.07 an hour, is that there are certain positions in the Canadian National services which are vacant and that they may be able to pick up some of these jobs.
What are some of the positions that these $3.07 an hour telegraphers are being told they can get? There are positions in dining cars at $1.99 per hour and positions as labourers at the Fort Garry hotel in Winnipeg at $1.28 per hour and so on. As a matter of fact the communication from the C.N.R. to these employees lists a whole page of various jobs that are open, but they all range from $1.28 per hour up to around $2 per hour. None of them equals the $3.07 an hour they are now receiving.
Undoubtedly the lay-offs the railways are making at Weston shops at Winnipeg, Ogden shops at Calgary, Angus shops at Montreal, and at Fort William and other places are due in part to automation and technological progress. If there is one overriding factor that faces us so far as the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act is concerned it is the need for inclusion in that legislation of something along the lines of the recommendations of the Freedman commission report. Yet despite the fact that for four years we have been told that this legislation was going to be amended and despite the fact
December 4, 1967

that the Freedman report has been around for two years we can still get nothing out of the minister or the government on this very important matter.
The Minister of Labour and his colleague who is now sitting with him, no doubt briefing him on a few procedural rules, go about the country making speeches. The theme of many of the Minister of Labour's speeches is positive industrial relations in the new environment. I have read many of them with interest and I suggest there is a need for positive industrial relations. There is a need for the government to get into the picture and help solve problems rather than fight battles, and I am using some of the minister's own words. One of his interesting statements was to the effect that there is a greater need for more fire prevention officers than firemen. This speech was made in Vancouver on November 7 of this year.
The minister also referred to the task force on labour relations set up by the Prime Minister and headed by Dan H. D. Woods. In the speech he made at Vancouver on November 7 the minister said he was hopeful that we would have the advantage of at least an interim report of the Woods task force within the next few months. If we are going to have any further delay in amending the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act we should at least wait until we have the benefit of the Woods report. But no, we have nothing advanced on the basis of the Freedman commission report and we have nothing proposed by the government to deal with the serious problems facing railroad telegraphers and the others I have mentioned. No attention is being paid to the suggestions that may have been made to the government by the Woods commission. Instead, we have this piece of legislation today. This is something that the Minister of Labour did not make clear, but it has been made clear by the Minister of Manpower and Immigration.
Therefore, I join with those who have said it is unfortunate this legislation is before us at this time. If it were to carry in its present form, far from doing the things the hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace and others hoped it might do I suggest it would make the job of the Canada Labour Relations Board impossible, and the reasonably satisfactory job of certification the board has done would become impossible. The net result of all these changes will not be good and will be inimical to labour relations in this country.
For these reasons I am glad the Minister of Labour has made it clear that instead of
Industrial Relations Act

I did not go into detail in this respect because I said the appropriate place to go into it in detail was in committee when the bill was before it. I dealt with the advisability and desirability of having

panels. Panels work well in other tribunals and there is no reason why they should not work here. The work of the board has, as I have already mentioned, increased by about 40 per cent, and having regard also to the changes that have taken place in industrialization in Canada there are good reasons why one panel of the board might not necessarily sit in Vancouver and another in the maritimes or the prairies of western Canada. There is no reason why the whole board should be taken out to these areas when it could sit as a panel, for example, where there is one matter of special interest to workers in the province of Quebec. We do not need the whole board to deal with that question. A panel could deal with the particular problem and another panel could be dealing with a matter of greater or lesser importance in another part of Canada.
The board is comprised of very busy men. It is true they usually sit for only two or three days each month. But they are busy executives as well as labour leaders. If they are to devote more and more time to the work of the board we are not likely to obtain the same calibre of men as we have had on the board. There is an advantage in having them sit in panels as do our courts. No one suggests that we do not get, from any one of the two or three divisions of the court of appeal of the province of Ontario or any one of the two or three divisions of the court of appeal of the province of British Columbia, the same justice as if the full court was sitting. There is an appeal from these courts to the Supreme Court of Canada. They frequently sit in divisions or panels to take care of situations that arise in different areas.
Nobody is trying to suggest for one moment, and certainly the Minister of Labour is not trying to do so, that one of the difficulties we are attempting to overcome in this legislation is not to make sure that not only will justice be done when the board decides something but that it shall appear to be done. That is one of the basic questions at issue today.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING GROUNDS, JURISDICTION, JUDGES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, for a long time divorce has rightly been a matter for concern to the Canadian people.
We felt duty bound, as a government, to reform divorce laws, to try and bring them more in line with the present social climate, without, for all that, runnng against the demands which are normal and worthy of respect of those who have reticences on that subject.
In trying to draft the present bill we met with two types of difficulties. The first, Mr. Chairman, is related to the field of federal-provincial relations and the second were mainly connected with the matter of conscience troubling a number of Canadians who expressed their views either through the various Churches or outside of them. Those Canadians are anxious, just as I am, to modernize the divorce laws of our society, while complying, at the same time, with that basic requirement that the present government considers essential, namely the necessity of surrounding the family with maximum protection.
With regard to the problems of the first group we proceeded as follows. Starting from the fact that under the Canadian constitution, divorce and marriage fall clearly and squarely within the jurisdiction of the central government we decided against shirking our responsibilities and we drew up an act dealing with the divorce problem, attaching to the solution of that problem measures of a corollary nature, that is which cannot be separated from the effects of a broken marriage as such.
We did so, Mr. Chairman, respecting as much as possible the current traditions and laws in the various provinces. The province of Quebec is known to have, in the field of marriage, a certain number of laws contained mainly in the Civil Code and forming part of the traditions in that province; it was essential that they should be respected.
But it should be remembered that other provinces too have had for a very long time their practices and their courts which, in the field of divorce had adopted certain procedures to which we wanted to bring some

degree of uniformity while bringing them up to date.
In regard to the second roup of problems, dealing with those I have included under the heading of problems of conscience and problems often referred to by religious organizations and by the churches, we have done two things. We have introduced in our legislation which Parliament will have the opportunity to see in a moment, special sections requiring the Court and the lawyers themselves to seek to reconcile the parties.
And we have also introduced in our legislation the concept of "the marriage breakdown" which is a concept that the churches themselves, in their joint briefs, have recommended.
This means, Mr. Chairman, that in this bill, we are taking into account, not only of the social problems which had to be solved but of the spiritual and moral problems and of the constitutional and legal problems.
IEnglish]
This bill, Mr. Chairman, represents an attempt to codify and extend the present laws of divorce applied in Canada along the lines recommended in the final report of the special joint committee on divorce dated June 27 last. That report contains some 21 recommendations respecting the subject of divorce and related matters. The bill adopts many of these recommendations, some of them in a modified form. In certain instances, the recommendations of the joint committee have not been adopted and with regard to other matters a somewhat different approach has been followed. We shall, of course, be considering these matters in more detail at later stages.
Speaking in more specific terms, I should say something about the grounds for divorce as contained in the bill. Hon. members will be aware that there has been a good deal of debate in recent times respecting the desirability of one comprehensive ground for divorce, namely marriage breakdown. My colleagues and I are aware that views to this effect are widely held by well-meaning people in this country, and indeed many of the Christian churches have advocated this approach.
While recognizing that this viewpoint has much to commend it, the bill has not been prepared on this basis, but retains the traditional marital offences as grounds for divorce, and includes as well a modified concept of marriage breakdown as a new ground for divorce. In so far as we are concerned
December 4, 1S67

with grounds for divorce, the bill can be fairly described as a composite one, recognising both marital offences and marriage breakdown. In this respect, the conclusions of the joint committee that breakdown could not constitute the sole and comprehensive ground for divorce, have been adopted.
[DOT] (8:10 p.ra.)
The new marriage breakdown principle contained in this bill, since it is to be administered by the existing courts in accordance with our well established judicial traditions, shies away from the vesting of any broad, undefined and uncontrolled discretion in the courts, in favour of a definition of legal rights by parliament. The result is that, the so-called inquest approach to divorce is rejected in favour of the customary judicial approach by which marriage breakdown will be established by evidence or proof of the existence of specified matrimonial situations.
For these reasons the government considers it desirable to maintain the administration of the divorce laws in the established courts of this country, to be administered pursuant to the rules or principles of law laid down by parliament, rather than invest a broad and uncontrolled administrative discretion in some new courts or tribunals.
Notwithstanding that hon. members will find that the grounds for divorce are being substantially extended by the bill, they will find that the bill is not simply or merely a divorce bill in the traditional sense. It is also a reconciliation bill, in that it imposes stated duties on both the legal profession and the courts in relation to the matter of reconciliation, and these provisions have been included in the hope that as many as possible of the broken marriages that come before the legal profession and the courts can be saved.
The government is fully conscious of the important public interest that exists in our society in relation to the maintenance and continuation of marriage and the family unit, where this is possible. The salvaging of marriages is at least as important as the burying of dead marriages that cannot be salvaged. However, a bill directed to the subject of divorce is not necessarily the most appropriate or only vehicle that can be employed to strengthen and give substance to the marriage estate. The government recognizes that financial assistance and encouragement may well be necessary to develop adequate counselling and other agencies that are necessary to deal with faltering or broken marriages, and it is the intention of the government to
Divorce Law Reform
keep this most important matter under continuous review.
The bill also contains provisions dealing with the law of domicile in so far as the existing law on this subject affects the position of married women in our society. An attempt has been made to place the married woman in a position equivalent to that of her husband for the purpose of obtaining a valid decree of divorce both within Canada and abroad.
No comprehensive bill on the subject of divorce would be complete without provisions for alimony, or pension alimentaire as the civil code of Quebec puts it, and for maintenance and the custody, care and upbringing of children. The bill therefore contains provisions dealing with these matters as corollary relief to petitions for divorce. Alimony, maintenance and custody orders made under the provisions of the statute will be enforceable by law throughout the whole of Canada upon being registered in the superior courts of this country.
The bill also contains provisions that will have the effect of abolishing parliamentary divorce, as we now understand it. In this regard we have departed a little bit from the report of the joint committee, but I think it is a step that this parliament is prepared to take. Therefore the Dissolution and Annulment of Marriages Act is to be repealed and divorce jurisdiction in respect of the provinces of Quebec and Newfoundland will be vested, at least temporarily, in a new divorce division of the Exchequer Court of Canada.
I mention that this jurisdiction might be temporary because the bill also contains a provision which will enable the jurisdiction to be transferred from the Exchequer Court to the Superior Court of Quebec and to the Supreme Court of Newfoundland by a proclamation issued by the governor in council on the respective recommendations of the lieutenant governors in council of those provinces. The idea is not to force upon any province a mode of procedure in the courts that it is not prepared to attain, but to suggest that, when these provinces are ready, we are ready, and that in the meantime we take out of parliament this outmoded way of proceeding, whereby divorces for two provinces had to be dealt with by one of the houses of parliament.
Consequential amendments are therefore proposed to the Exchequer Court Act. These amendments will establish a divorce division of that court, with special provision being

December 4, 1967
Divorce Law Reform
made so that any person who holds, or who has held office as a judge of a superior or county court, may by special request sit and act as a judge of the divorce division. A special provision for the remuneration of such persons has been included to assure the judicial independence of such persons at all times. I am sure hon. members will realize that this is the reason we are proceeding now by way of resolution rather than by introducing a bill right away.
The bill will also contain detailed appeal provisions and a number of other matters that do not need to be discussed at this stage. However, it should be mentioned that there is a clause in the bill which will prevent it from coming into force for at least three months after it has been assented to. This provision has been inserted to permit the holding of such discussions or conferences as may be necessary to facilitate implementation of the new laws throughout the country.

I should like to mention here, Mr. Chairman, that such period of consultation should also allow the federal government and the provinces to discuss an extremely important other problem, that of judicial separation.
Hon. members will see that in this bill, we have dealt with divorce only; the problem of judicial separation has been, for the time being, I hope, temporarily set aside. Hon. members will readily realize the reason why we have chosen to proceed in this way. If we had included the matter of judicial separation in this bill, as it would have been easy to do when drafting this legislation, this bill would have raised very complicated problems of implementation in a number of provinces.
I do not refer here, Mr. Chairman, to constitutional problems because, although the matter is debatable, we feel that the judicial separation comes under federal jurisdiction, since it falls readily-

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like my first words on this matter to be those of relief and pleasure at being in this house when, at long last, a measure of reform of our divorce law is to be brought before the house. I should like to congratulate the minister on having the honour to be the one who is introducing this legislation.
The archaic divorce laws we have had have caused untold misery to many thousands of Canadians. This measure of reform is long overdue. As the minister pointed out, parliament has had jurisdiction over this matter for over 100 years and yet has never 27053-317*
Divorce Law Reform
boldly exercised it in any way. It has legislated in a piecemeal way, usually merely by introducing the existing laws of England at particular stages of our history.
Mr. Chairman, not having seen the bill, I do not think at this stage it would be appropriate for me to enlarge on this matter at any length or comment at any length on what the minister has said. I think perhaps it is a truism, although one which I think ought to be said, that, notwithstanding the pessimists, marriage is thriving in Canada, fortunately very many Canadians find in the marriages and families a very great source of happiness. All of us must be concerned that we do not do anything to undermine or defeat the institution of marriage.
I believe we also must recognize that, despite any individual views of our own, none of us has any right to impose on others views which no longer are socially acceptable. One thing on which most, if not all, of us will agree is that the present law is entirely unsatisfactory. The single ground of adultery is a superficial and inadequate ground. It leads not only to the commission of the offence but also to fabrication and perjury which are a disgrace to the courts. There is also the problem of those persons who, finding marriage unacceptable or impossible, form common law unions, stable unions which can never be normal unions so long as divorce is what it is at the present time. There is the problem of children of such unions.
The minister has said that by and large the report of the joint committee, on which I happened to be a member, will be largely accepted. I cannot refrain, however, from expressing a measure of regret that the legislation is not accepting the clearcut choice which exists between the two basic theories in respect of the dissolution of marr:age. One is that the grounds of matrimonial misconduct upon which divorce can be based should be enlarged. The other is that the dissolution of marriage should be based upon the declaration that the marriage is dead; that is, that the marriage has broken down, and that there exists no longer any hope of reconciliation.
This is not divorce by consent; it is divorce by judicial decision. The mind of the judge would be directed to the question of whether there is hope of reconciliation, and not to the hopeless and futile exercise of deciding whose misconduct was responsible for the breakdown of the marriage. We would have much preferred to see the government accept the recommendation made initially by the

December 4, 1967
Divorce Law Reform
United Church and concurred in by many other churches. This is the recommendation that breakdown be the sole ground for dissolution of marriage. When I say "we" I am not of course speaking for my own party; I am speaking for some of us who were members of the committee, who looked into this matter and heard the representations which were presented. The reasons for stressing breakdown are many. I will not enlarge on them here. I feel, under the compromise choice that the government apparently has adopted, that lawyers will still advise their clients to go on the simple ground of matrimonial misconduct and that we will still be back to the same old questions.

speechtext: Would the hon. member permit a question. As a lawyer, does he not think it is preferable that parliament should indicate to the courts the grounds which the lawmakers themselves feel indicative of a breakdown, rather than leave to the court the administrative freedom to make this kind of decision; is there not a question of legal propriety involved in this?

subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING GROUNDS, JURISDICTION, JUDGES, ETC.
speechtext:
I think not. I believe the courts are perfectly competent to determine whether the marriage is in fact dead, for the many different reasons which may have resulted in this unhappy outcome. I think once you specify grounds you limit the grounds. Once the marriage has broken down, then I suggest the marriage is dead and it is the duty of the court to dissolve it.
[DOT] (8:30 p.m.)
Let me suggest that the basic ground involved in the breakdown of a marriage should be the finding of a court that there is no hope of reconciliation. The causes for that situation may be very many, including adultery, cruelty, desertion or a hundred and one other things. Once this fact, the fact of breakdown has been established, whatever the reason may be, then the court should be empowered to take action on that finding.
It is my personal belief that the courts can determine this question just as well as they determine today whether a mother or father under certain circumstances will make the best and most responsible individual to raise the children. This is a very general question, but I believe the courts can determine it, and should have assistance from social workers and others who have studied the background of the marriage in question.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

Could I ask the hon. member another question? If our bill included the
[Mr. Brewin.!
marriage breakdown concept would the hon. member see any objection to keeping also the other concept of marital offence?

speechtext: Yes. I wish I had time to go into this at length, and perhaps on second reading I shall attempt to do so. I recommend that the minister should look again, as perhaps he has already done, at the very excellent survey of this whole subject called "Putting Asunder", which is a report made by a committee appointed by the Archbishop of Canterbury. That committee comprised a number of judges, sociologists, lawyers, groups of doctors and other people who, having had a law which enlarged the grounds for matrimonial misconduct on which divorce was based since 1937, came to the conclusion after careful study that this is not the best approach, but that the best approach was based on the principle of marriage breakdown, the other things being symptoms rather than causes.

But there are rights of appeal, and jurisprudence can be developed on this subject just as well as on other subjects, such as the meaning of cruelty. I take it that the act will include cruelty as one ground for divorce. This is also a vague and general provision, yet the courts have to determine what is cruelty. One judge may recognize cruelty much more easily than another. I think this is inevitable in any human judicial system. I do not think this is a good enough reason to reject the concept of marriage breakdown.
I was attempting to deal briefly with a summary of my reasons for thinking the marriage breakdown concept is the best approach. In my view, and in the view of others, this system gets away from the present requirement for sordid proof of adultery. That is my first reason. The second is that it would afford in all cases the necessity of the court seeking a reconciliation, or at least the determination that the parties cannot be reconciled. I had hoped to hear the
December 4, 1967

minister say that some such provision would be included in the bill, but I cannot judge the bill until I see it. In any event, the whole concept of breakdown necessarily involves in almost every case a judicial investigation of the question of reconciliation.
Finally, this concept gets away from the false notion of a breakdown of marriage based upon matrimonial misconduct where one party blames the other, which is totally unreal I suggest in 99 out of 100 cases. The view I have expressed is not my own view or the view of a few people. It was supported before the committee by the United Church of Canada, the Anglican Church of Canada, the National Council of Women, the Canadian Mental Health Association, the Canadian Jewish Congress, the Canadian Comittee on the Status of Women and a number of lawyers and individuals who appeared and gave evidence. It is not in any light-hearted way that we put this suggestion forward.
I can understand that it is perhaps difficult to break away from traditions of the past, but I should like to express my regret that the government has not seen fit to accept what we believe to be the best approach, and has accepted what we consider to be the second best approach. This is not the time to go into this matter in great detail, but I should like to give the committee the definition taken by the law reform commission in England as to what a good divorce law should be. Good divorce law should seek to achieve the following objectives: to buttress rather than undermine the stability of marriage and, when regrettable the marriage has broken down, to enable the empty legal shell to be destroyed with a maximum of fairness and a minimum of bitterness, distress and humiliation.
I believe this bill will go some way in that direction, but there are improvements which can be made. It is my hope that the minister will be flexible, as I think he usually is, and will listen to suggestions that may be made at the committee stage. I understand there is to be provision in the bill for dealing with problems regarding the maintenance of a divorced spouse and children. This is as it should be and I hope there will be effective means for enforcement of any order that may be made in that respect.
We in this party and the people of Canada generally await with interest the specific wording of the bill. I have criticized the choice of the government and I will stick to that criticism. I regret that it has accepted something I think is second best. Neverthe-
