Mr. Chairman, I would like to say a few words about this bill related to our divorce laws.
If I understood the minister's remarks correctly a few minutes ago, he stated that his bill was not meant to promote divorce as such, but rather to improve the current situation in Canada.
Now, if this is the purpose of the resolution and the bill to follow, I should say immediately that I support the minister, for I, too, believe that our divorce laws may need some improvement and amendment.
However, to improve the situation in a permanent and efficient manner, the government should particularly try to eliminate or prevent the causes of misunderstanding between members of the same family. Now, I think that poverty and destitution are the main factors of disunion, which unfortunately lead too often to a separation or a divorce. Those are two of the main reasons for disunion or misunderstanding, and I think the government could eliminate those points further by adopting truly social measures.
There are other causes as well. For exam-1 pie, I often see heads of families forced to go quite a distance to earn a living for their families and they are therefore unable to go and see their wife and children very often.
In my opinion, Mr. Chairman, that is often another cause of disagreement and quarrel within large families, and I think a way might be found to prevent this. Today, heads of families are often forced to work far from home, in large as well as small towns. Moreover, the wives leave to seek outside work in order to make ends meet. Quite often, the husband and wife do not work the same hours; one works in the daytime, another at night, and sometimes vice versa. This means that sometimes they do not see each other for weeks. I think that there also social organizations should exert themselves on correcting this irregular situation.
There is a third cause which I would like to mention to the minister to-night, I mean alcoholism which is already widespread and is spreading even more, and which is a main cause of divorce, of discord. Alcoholism is spreading more and more in our country and

December 4, 1967
Divorce Law Reform
we notice that it sows the seeds of discord in homes and entails poverty. So when the wife-sometimes it is the husband, because alcoholism is spreading more and more among women-is weary of such of life, she is prompted to request divorce.
[DOT] (8:40 p.m.)
So, I think we could almost completely eliminate the situations due to alcoholism by organizing an efficient war on this national plague. I understand that the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Benson) would find a reduction in his revenue, but I think that the whole population of Canada would gain considerably.
The best way to fight divorce is to eliminate its causes as much as possible. Obviously, there will always be some, but several can be eliminated if we work at it efficiently.
Whatever the bill the minister may introduce in the house, I hope that he will respect the sacred nature of marriage, the very basis of any society. In fact, if we go back in history we realize that the peoples, who are said to be the least civilized, attach great importance to matrimony and were respectful of it. So, we, who claim to be civilized, should be capable of bringing down the necessary legislation, effective legislation to improve the situation of our Canadian families.

The hon. member for Greenwood has flogged one ground for divorce which has been pretty well kicked around during the year of committee discussion, that is the addition of a brand new approach, namely that of marriage breakdown as a specific and individual ground.
I wish to point out to the committee that this has been thoroughly touted and that the ideas of the hon. member for Greenwood, attractive though they may appear to be, have been shot down by a rather impressive commission of hard-nosed people in the United Kingdom who have examined the problem of marriage breakdown. The ideas that the hon. member put forward have also been snowed under by any group that I have heard discussing this matter in the House of Commons.
But be that as it may, whether one considers marriage breakdown as a ground for divorce, or recognizes the recommendations contained in the report, I would suggest that in examining all the possible grounds for divorce the only one that has been left out is that of people living together in conditions of extreme incompatibility. 1 believe that every

other situation which could arise is covered first, in the committee report, where it mentions adultery, rape, sodomy, bestiality, cruelty, desertion, non support, bigamy, non-consummation; and then there is recognition that marriage breakdown can arise for five reasons, namely illness, criminality, imprisonment, alcoholism, drug addiction, desertion and separation. The second point deals with the rights of women and children, and I am glad the Minister of Justice clearly indicated that these are ancillary rights which can be dealt with in divorce cases.
The third point on which I should like to comment briefly is one on which action is now being taken. The woman in this country have been at a disadvantage in the past by being tied to her husband's domicile, with the exception of the 1930 amendment regarding desertion, and it is a welcome change that this defect in the legislation is being overcome.
The fourth point is the question of court procedures. We are pleased that the Quebec and Newfoundland cases will be booted off parliament hill. The last time they were swiped they were kicked from the Senate building over to the west block and in my opinion there is no reason why they should not go into some building outside parliament hill. I share the hopes of the Minister of Justice that the Quebec and Newfoundland cases will eventually find their way into the courts of the respective provinces. I think the formula he suggests in that regard is an appropriate one. It is difficult not to support it in view of the fact that it must cost the litigants who come before us anywhere from $1,000 to $1,500 above and beyond what they would pay in the courts of other provinces if they were not living in Quebec or Newfoundland. Since there is little enough money in any marriage, if there is any money to be spread around it should go to the women and children and to the establishment of new homes. This is a step in the right direction. I hope the minister has included the hearing of cases in county courts, as I gather is the case. The committee felt that this would make it financially easier for the petitioner to have their cases heard.
Finally, the fifth point is on the reconciliation and saving of marriages. I must confess

that I think the committee did not get its teeth properly into the subject. I believe action should be taken in the house with regard to the question of saving marriages. Mr. Chairman, I intend to be very brief and to add only a few remarks to what has already been said on the important resolution before us. This is a historic night for thousands of Canadians, when finally the parliament of Canada is devoting itself to passing a resolution dealing with divorce reform.
Many of us on both sides of the house have worked for many years toward amending our laws on divorce. Speaking of myself, shortly after I became a member of the house I joined many others in introducing private members bills on the subject, in the hope of getting the government to take some action in this regard and to introduce divorce reform measures.
[DOT] (9:00 p.m.)
I wish to congratulate in the fullest posi-ble terms the joint committee of the Senate
[Mr. McCleave.l
and the House of Commons which has examined this subject, and to compliment the Minister of Justice and the government for having the courage to deal with the subject and to introduce a bill. It has always been said, certainly to me, that divorce reform was some sort of Canadian sacred cow with which politicians could not deal. I know that I have had many politicians with long experience say to me: Young man, you should not talk about divorce reform or urge that we deal with it; it will get you into nothing but trouble. I do not believe it is a sacred cow. I am delighted to learn that the Minister of Justice does not think so, and has had the courage to present a resolution covering a very comprehensive divorce reform measure.
In the past, of course, this government has attacked a number of other things that have been regarded by Canadian politicians as sacred cows, things with which governments should not deal. I refer to the flag, the anthem and many other subjects. I am delighted to learn that the Prime Minister and the Minister of Justice are prepared to tackle controversial subjects which it was always thought governments would be well advised to leave alone. All of us who have had any dealings with divorce, either as lawyers, members of parliament or members of a committee, know the tremendous heartaches, hardships and suffering which result from our present stupid and antiquated divorce laws.
We have in British Columbia, the province from which I come, a divorce act which came into force on November 18, 1857. In my view it is one of the greatest centennial presents we could give to the people of Canada when, 110 years later, this parliament is finally bringing into force a new divorce act. As I say, we have been dealing with a divorce act in British Columbia, and in most of Canada, that is 110 years old. I know there are hundreds of thousands of Canadians who will express their thanks to the Minister of Justice and to this parliament for finally getting around to dealing with this subject of divorce reform. There are many Canadians, I believe, who feel that what takes place in this chamber is quite removed from the ordinary problems of life, and that parliament is sometimes rather remote from the ordinary difficulties many people have. I believe that in this measure we are debating tonight we are showing the Canadian people that we, as
December 4, 1967

individual members of parliament, are concerned with the problems which affect ordinary people, such as deserted wives and uncared for children.
As I say, I should like in a very few minutes to record my appreciation to the government and the minister for introducing this measure. We are of course discussing a resolution which precedes a bill, and should not deal with the details of the bill which will follow. I only hope the bill will receive speedy passage through this house, so the people who are suffering under our present divorce laws will be able to receive some relief under the new act.

Mr. Chairman, I want to congratulate parliament on the step being taken tonight. During the last ten years we have sat in this house for many hours discussing the problem of divorce. I think we have raised this problem, from the point where divorce was a dirty word which no one would use to the point where the situation became so bad that all the news media in the country were pointing out to members of parliament that we were many years behind the times, and the need for reform was urgent. Reform was acceptable to the people but members of parliament were still dragging their feet.
There were many members of parliament who participated in the divorce blockade a number of years ago. I think of the hon. member for Halifax who spoke a few minutes ago, who took one side, and I took the other. I believe this controversy brought about the acceptance by parliament of the fact that the problem should have been solved many years before. I can remember a prime minister one night almost getting down on bended knee and talking about the 1500 people who were involved in divorce bills. He said the fact we were holding up these divorces might mean many children would be born out of wedlock. Well, Mr. Chairman, I think the government has finally decided to do something for these people. They have decided to take a look at the neglect that has occurred in the field of social legislation for many years, and which has produced hardship for many people.
Let me say that on many occasions the hon. member for Skeena and I wondered whether or not we were right in taking advantage of the very unusual circumstances which allowed us to hold up these divorce bills, in the hope that eventually parliament would reach the conclusion something had to be done about the situation. I am happy to
Divorce Law Reform
have been able to be in this parliament when the government finally decided to introduce this measure. I certainly appreciate the things that have been done by many people over the years. I am thinking of people in the news media who wrote articles and who appeared on television interviews to discuss this controversial problem. Eventually every person in the country obtained sufficient knowledge to enable him to decide whether or not to support our archaic social laws, or whether they should be changed.
I am proud also that the present Minister of Justice has continued a concession made by a former minister of justice. It was the late justice minister Favreau who introduced the first change by establishing procedures for divorce in the Exchequer Court, rather than the parliamentary procedure, thus making possible the end of the blockade. This course had been advocated many years before by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, who has always been impressed with the idea of having* the Exchequer Court as the divorce court for those provinces that did not have divorce courts.
Mr. Chairman, we are delighted with this resolution; but we should also speak about the other social problems we must face. I am thinking of the discussions that took place during those years when we fought for divorce reform. I know there were many members who believed as firmly as I did that divorce reform was absolutely necessary. During that period the news media were willing to publicize many of these social problems, and I am pleased to note the Minister of Justice is going to do something about them.
I can remember the time when "divorce" was a bad word and we used to pass divorce bills 100 at a time. Nobody cared about them, and cared less about whether the children would have any maintenance. I remember one case in which the hon. member for Timmins and I were interested. The husband had accumulated a million dollars by investing $25,000 that his wife had, but in attempting to get rid of her he was providing nothing for her. If he had been successful he would have turned her out on the street without a cent, and this because of the action of this house.
[DOT] (9:10 p.m.)
I think it is safe to say that abortion is another matter the minister will have to look at. I am not referring to aborting a mother

December 4, 1967
Divorce Law Reform
ior clinical reasons; I am referring to abortion in cases where it is a question of the woman not wanting to have a baby.
We will have to look at the problem of homosexuality from the point of view of at least allowing acts between two consenting adults conducted in private, as is now the case in Britain. I am also sure we will come to legalize birth control. Another area we will have to look at is what in my opinion are the crazy social laws of the church which were introduced four or five hundred years ago. These were enacted into legislation in Britain, and we have inherited them. The province of Quebec is even further behind because they inherited similar laws from France, and the Napoleonic code was even more archaic in outlook that the British law.
Since we have provided some relief in the matter of divorce, as the hon. member for Greenwood stated I think we might as well go all the way. When a partnership breaks down it might as well be dissolved. That is true of any partnership. I sympathize with the Minister of Justice. He did ask the hon. member for Greenwood whether he thought the courts were sufficiently equipped to handle the question of marriage breakdown. Personally I should like marriage breakdown to be the only ground for divorce. It cannot be an added ground; either it is a legal partnership which is continuing, or it is one that has broken down and should be dissolved. I do not think you can have it both ways.
I too am wondering whether the courts are sufficiently equipped to provide the kind of surveillance that would be required in cases of marriage breakdown. This also raises the question of what the courts have been doing hitherto. I have talked to a lawyer who has handled hundreds of divorce cases and it is his opinion that less than 10 per cent of these cases actually involve adultery. Everyone in court has known that the litigants have been telling lies. I feel safe in making that statement because at one time the hon. member for Skeena and I sent out 1,400 letters to respondents and corespondents, and we found that at least 400 of the names were fictitious. Some addresses did not even exist. I am sure the judges who tried these cases also knew they were false, and that most of the cases were rigged. Even where adultery was involved the woman in question was not the intended future partner of the respondent, but a woman who had been hired for a few dollars. Everything was a nice neat little package.

I am very proud that the minister appears at last to have taken the step of deciding that the federal government will have a say in the disposition and maintenance of children of divorced parents. Children are part of a marriage, and under the terms of the British North American Act they come under the jurisdiction of the federal government in such cases.
I wish to say very little more, Mr. Chairman, except that it gives me a great deal of personal satisfaction that the government is now introducing this legislation. I suggest to the minister that he will find himself in the same position as the former minister of justice, both of them being Catholics and coming from the province of Quebec. We were very worried about the position that might be taken by other agencies in that province, but I was pleased to find, after talking to the former minister of justice that he had not received one complaint about the change that was made during his term of office. For 50 years advisers to the minister of justice had argued that divorce by parliament was an exception to the rule: that divorce through the courts was not a right. But as I anticipated, the minister experienced no complaints, because the social reality of the situation demanded a change.
I think the minister has given a Christmas present to the 500,000 people that the Canadian Bar Association state are engaging in common law relationships. The value of this the minister will not realize until he starts to receive the mail that I am sure will flow when the legislation is passed. I am also sure that these relationships that have been established but not legalized will in most cases be legalized, and will probably become lasting unions which will be a credit to Canada. If the minister of immigration has been happy over the years at the arrangements that have been made to legalize the position of Chinese immigrants, I am sure the pride of the Minister of Justice will be that much greater because of the role that this legislation will play in the lives of a large number of people.
Parliament itself is to be congratulated on this proposed change, as are the members of the divorce committee and the members of the press who gave the buildup that has been necessary to bring about this social change. I could single out many who made a great contribution to the step that members of parliament are taking tonight. The role played by the communications media in establishing this social change has often been ignored.

That area over which I had the pleasure of flying last summer has been developed over quite a number of years. It will be recalled that in 1898, it was the scene of the Gold Rush; it will also be remembered that in 1943, the Alaska highway was built through it. But it is mostly since 1947, due to exploration work for gas and oil in the territories to the south and to the gradual extension of that exploration and development to the north, that this area has become important and will become even more so in the future.
As I said earlier, Mr. Speaker, it is a matter of defining the land boundary rather than changing it.
As early as 1898, the federal Department of the Interior had started the work, which lasted from 1899 to 1908, but most of the surveying has been done since 1943. In that year, the Privy Council, with the agreement of British Columbia, instituted the commission on the boundary between British Columbia, the Yukon and the Northwest Territories, instructing it to survey those boundaries and to report to the parliament of Canada and to the legislature of the province of British Columbia.
The commission comprised the surveyor general of Canada, as usual, and the surveyor general of British Columbia. The commission undertook the survey of the boundary in 1945 and pursued the work from 1945 to 1959. Six hundred and twenty-two miles of boundary were surveyed; there are 39 miles more to survey at the western extremity. Those 39 miles lie on extremely difficult glacial terrain which holds no immediate interest for the mining industry in particular.
When the work was completed, the commission wrote its report, dated February 15, 1966. This report included a map showing the location of the surveyed boundaries and the monuments placed on the ground for site identification. This document was tabled in the House of Commons on December 14, 1966.
It may perhaps be asked-I see that some hon. members are absent, fortunately


-under what constitutional authority the federal government engaged in boundary surveying. The answer to that will be found in the British North America Act of 1871. Indeed, the act provides that the parliament of Canada may from time to time, with the consent of the legislature of any province, increase, diminish, or otherwise alter the limits of such province, upon such terms and conditions as may be agreed to by the said legislature, i.e., with the consent of provincial authorities.
By applying these provisions now, we can substitute the line of monuments on the ground for the abstract mathematical concept of the sixtieth parallel of north latitude,, mentioned in particular in the Imperial Act of 1866.
The British Columbia legislature passed an act entitled: An Act of Consent respecting the Adoption of the British Columbia-Yukon-Northwest Territories Boundary, which was sanctioned on March 23, 1967. Therefore, the conditions imposed by the British North America Act of 1871 have been fully complied with, and there only remains for the house to pass, if it will, the bill introduced tonight.

Following the gold rush and the rapid increase of population in the Yukon territory, and the establishment of that territory out of the Northwest Territories, it became necessary to delineate the line of demarcation between the province of British Columbia and the new territory.
It is an interesting observation with respect to the difficulties of Canadian terrain that the process of marking out the boundaries on the ground has been taking place, off and on, ever since that time. IMMIGRATION-BRITISH COLUMBIA-NONPARTICIPATION IN REFUGEE SETTLEMENT PLAN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in 1960 during world refugee year the then Conservative government embarked upon a program of bringing, initially, 100 tubercular families to Canada and asked the provinces to participate with the government on a proportionate basis. The premier of British Columbia, the same gentleman who today is the premier of that province, spurned that offer, refused to participate in the joint venture and after a few agonizing and embarrassing moments of reflection embarked upon a grandiose scheme to buy food in British Columbia and distribute it to the starving peoples of the world. In fact, in a press release in May of 1960 the establishment of the world relief fund of the province of British Columbia was announced, and the then minister of health and welfare, Eric Martin, became its chairman. An amount of $50,000 was contributed by the provincial government by a special warrant and a commitment was made to match, dollar for dollar, every dollar that was contributed by the general public up to an amount of $475,000 which, if the full contribution were made, would raise about $1 million.
The world relief fund of the provincial government was heralded with great fanfare when it was announced, and then was immediately forgotten. Articles written in newspapers since that time have all pointed to the fact that the $50,000 has not been touched, and that the province has not embarked upon any world relief fund.
As late as this year Mr. Tom Berger, M.L.A., who was a member of this house, asked some questions in the British Columbia legislature as to whether or not the money was still there. The answer he received was that the $50,000 was still there, that no payments had been made out of it and that it did not seem likely that any payments would be made from that fund. We do not know where it went; it is still there in trust. However, this points up the deceit which the premier of British Columbia used at that time to cover up his lack of desire to participate in a very worthwhile program to assist the tubercular refugees from other countries to come to Canada, where they may receive some medical and other assistance.
The other day the Minister of Manpower and Immigration announced a government sponsored program to bring 50 handicapped
December 4, 1967

Proceedings on Adjournment Motion refugees to Canada, most of whom are tubercular cases. He announced that eight provincial governments would participate with the federal government in bringing these unfortunate souls to Canada, where medical and other assistance may be provided for them. Once again the province of British Columbia has failed to participate with the government of Canada in this very humane and worthwhile venture.
I submit that this indicates a lack of interest on the part of the premier of my own province, in an extremely worth-while venture. All I can do is to hope that publicity will be given to the manner in which he has treated his own world relief fund which he announced in 1960; the fact that it did not get off the ground and that no one in his government tried to make it work; the fact that Eric Martin, the then minister of health and welfare admitted he was at fault in not doing anything to bring the program into effect; and the fact that the premier has once again spurned the participation of his province in an extremely worth-while and humanitarian project.
Perhaps all we can do is to hope that if these facts are given some publicity the premier of British Columbia will be shamed, together with the government of Canada, into participating in this venture, and in giving some assistance to unfortunate people from other countries.

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT-VANCOUVER- EMPLOYMENT OF POSTAL TRUCK DRIVERS
POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT-VANCOUVER- EMPLOYMENT OF POSTAL TRUCK DRIVERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise tonight to put a question


to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Nicholson) concerning the plight of the employees of a company in Vancouver which, for many years, as a private company has hauled the mail for the post office, and which company bears the romantic name of the Pony Express. I want to turn first to a letter which I received from an executive of that company on April 30, and which reads in part:
-the Canada Postal Department proposed to enter into the trucking business July 1 in the city of Vancouver by taking over 25 per cent of the work at present held by a long established trucking company with a view to possibly doing all the work.
When I received that letter I promptly wrote to the Postmaster General (Mr. Cote) and asked him for particulars of the matter. I received from him a letter which I should like to read in part:
The present practice of handling this mail has been done by contract and not by post office employees except in the city of Windsor, Ontario. Long range plans of the Post Office Department have included for some time a study of the economics involved in taking over the service ourselves. The strike by employees of the Montreal contractor early in December last year emphasized the vulnerability of the department in this area. While the Post Office Department was in no way involved in the dispute between mail chauffeurs and the contractor, nevertheless, the strike resulted in considerable disruption of the mail service not only in Montreal but across the country because Montreal is a key distributing point. Preliminary study would indicate that it may well be more efficient and more economical to have the department operate its own vehicle service.
The only satisfactory method of establishing the economics and practicality of doing the job ourselves is to conduct an experiment and we picked two major post offices-Montreal and Vancouver- as suitable for pilot plant study.
I now want to refer, sir, to a further letter I have received from an officer of the Pony Express company regarding this contract. It reads in part:
Pony Express Limited has been the mail contractor since 1911, and despite the fact that they, the employees, consider membership in the teamster's union essential for their welfare, not once has the mail in the greater Vancouver area been delayed or held up since the company contracted to do any of the services under discussion. In fact, to the contrary, with the aid of the teamster's union and despite many local labour disputes and strikes, mail at all times has been delivered by Pony Express couriers, when in many instances post office employees have refused to cross picket lines.
At another point, the letter reads:
I understand that Mr. Cote has stated that "in the interests of progress" any Pony Express employee was free to apply for the position of postal chauffeur. I ask you, sir, is it logical or sensible for any man in this province to apply for the same job at a lower rate of pay?
December 4, 1967	COMMONS
I have learned recently that this experiment, as it is called by the Postmaster General, went forward despite the protests of this company, a company that has served so well and despite troubles that have existed in the postal department. Those who have been deprived of their jobs have made application to the Post Office Department for the position of postal chauffeur. I now find that some members have had their applications to become postal chauffeurs rejected, on the basis that they live outside the area served by the Vancouver post office, although they have worked for Pony Express for many years while living at these addresses, and while handling these duties in a satisfactory manner.
What I want to ask is this: I ask the Minister of Labour tonight what can be done specifically for these employees. I hope he will be able to give a satisfactory answer.
The other question I want to put to the government is this: Why is it necessary to continue with an experiment of this nature in order to correct what is considered to be a disruptive situation between labour and management in the Montreal area? Why must we in Vancouver, where the work of hauling the mail has never been handled more satisfactorily, be penalized because of these particular difficulties? I would ask the government to review the whole matter and not to deprive of work the Pony Express, and those employees who have worked so faithfully carrying the Queen's mail. I ask the minister to see what can be done to right what is an obvious injustice.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. R. Nicholson (Minister of Labour):
maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT-VANCOUVER- EMPLOYMENT OF POSTAL TRUCK DRIVERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to deal with that part of the question which is directed to the Minister of Labour and to say that I have had occasion to investigate the circumstances referred to by the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra. I am convinced that those employees of the Pony Express who are affected in this particular case have done an outstanding job over the years. In my opinion, based on my investigations to date, it

Proceedings on Adjournment Motion would be most unfortunate if the five or six employees of the Pony Express who live in what I might call the metropolitan area of Vancouver are not able to perform their work as postal chauffeurs by reason of the fact that they do not happen to live in that part of the postal area referred to by the hon. member.
I might say that not only have I taken the matter up as Minister of Labour-because an important principle relating to employment is involved here-but I have also taken up the matter as a member of parliament representing that part of Vancouver where the main post office in question is located. I have had a particular interest in the matter and have taken it up with the deputy postmaster general and with the chairman of the public service commission with a view, I hope, to assuring that the five or six employees of Pony Express will not be deprived of their opportunity to qualify as postal servants in the employ of the Post Office Department.
This is particularly important today in view of the trend toward urbanization. People in outlying communities today find that through no fault of their own they are engulfed by neighbouring metropolitan areas or surrounding municipalities. It would seem unfair to deprive these people-after all, they are all Canadians-of their right to work, by virtue of some regulation that has been followed by the Civil Service Commission over a period of years.
I can assure the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra I am encouraged to believe some progress is being made, but I cannot give him the affirmative answer he would like to hear tonight. With regard to the second part of the question, which was not referred to in the matter about which I was given notice to speak tonight, the only person who could deal effectively with it is the Postmaster General, who unfortunately is not here.
